title: The child on the leaf
hook: a sage is breathed in and out by a child on a banyan leaf; why Hindus see time as cycles that rest in God
carry: time breathes in cycles, and rests in god
tomorrow: why is half of Shiva a woman?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna's restless mind, and the out-breath: four counts in, six counts out. Your line was Arjuna's wind: the mind follows the breath. Today, a sage who gets breathed in by a god, and the pause at the top of every breath.
screen: `ARJUNA'S WIND: THE MIND FOLLOWS THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The world has ended. Not in fire: in water. A sage named Markandeya is swimming alone in a dark ocean with no shore, for what feels like ages. Then, on the water, a banyan tree, and on one of its leaves, a baby. Glowing, calm, sucking his own toe. Markandeya swims closer. The baby breathes in, and the sage is pulled into his body like a mosquito on the wind.
screen: `THE WORLD UNDER WATER.` → `A BABY ON A BANYAN LEAF.` → `BREATHED IN LIKE A MOSQUITO.`

segments.voice: Inside the child, Markandeya finds everything. Mountains, rivers, cities, even his own little hermitage. The whole world, alive inside one small body. Then the baby breathes out, and the sage tumbles back into the dark water, and there's the child again on the leaf, smiling. This is from the Bhagavata Purana, and the child is Vishnu. Here's the teaching under it, one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: time moves in cycles. The world isn't made once and finished. It comes out, lives, dissolves, and rests in God, and then comes out again, age after age. Between worlds, it's often pictured as Vishnu resting on the great ocean. Nothing is lost there; everything is held, waiting for the next breath. Now the word. Kumbhaka, from kumbha, a clay water jar: the breath resting still, like water in a jar. Every breath has two small pauses, one at the top after the in-breath, and one at the bottom after the out-breath. Some teachers like to read them as tiny echoes of that great rest. Keep it gentle: two soft counts, no clamping the throat. The old yoga texts describe long holds, but those were taught one to one, by a teacher watching closely. If a pause makes you anxious or short of air, skip it. If you're pregnant, or have high blood pressure, or a heart or lung condition, leave the holds out and just notice where the pauses would be. For Hindus, a stop isn't the end of the story. It's the world resting in God before the next breath.
screen: `THE WHOLE WORLD INSIDE HIM.` · `TIME MOVES IN CYCLES.` · `BETWEEN WORLDS, IT RESTS IN GOD.` · `KUMBHA — A WATER JAR.` · `TWO SOFT COUNTS, NEVER A STRAIN.` · then, large: `TIME BREATHES IN CYCLES, AND RESTS IN GOD.`

segments.voice: Breathe in for four and rest at the top for two, then breathe out for six and rest at the bottom for two, and let the next breath come. If the holds feel easy, keep them; if not, just notice where the top and bottom are without stopping, and either way is the practice. Look for the still point, like the child resting on the leaf.
Kumbhaka. From kumbha, a water jar. The pause in the breath, where everything rests for a moment.
Hold on to it: time breathes in cycles, and rests in God. Markandeya was breathed out to see it. Day ninety-nine, in the books.

screen: `DAY 99 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY IS HALF OF SHIVA A WOMAN?`

howItsDone: Hindu teaching pictures time in great cycles of creation and dissolution, with the world resting in God between them; images of the child on the banyan leaf recall Markandeya's vision. In yoga, kumbhaka, gentle breath retention, is taught gradually by a teacher.

fork.setup: a friend hears that Hindus believe the world ends and begins again, and says that sounds bleak. what fits today's teaching?
options: it isn't bleak: between worlds, everything rests in God, like the world Markandeya found held inside the child.
it means the world ends forever, so nothing really matters.
it's only a poem about seasons; Hindus don't really teach cycles of time.
fork.reveal: in Hindu teaching, dissolution isn't loss. the world rests in God, then is breathed out again.

original.note: Sanskrit: from kumbha, a water jar; the breath held still.

trapdoor: what you thought: the world has one beginning and one end.
what it means: it's breathed out, lives, and rests in God before the next breath, like the child breathing Markandeya in and out.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 12.8–12.9 (Markandeya's vision of the child on the banyan leaf); the cycles of creation and pralaya; kumbhaka in hatha yoga.

chat.says: practice drive w dad. i froze at a stop sign and literally stopped breathing lol. nani said 'that's not the end, beta, that's the pause.' what does she MEAN
options: it's from Markandeya's story: even the end of the world is only a rest in God before the next breath. a stop isn't the end.
she means hold your breath on purpose next time, as long as you can.
nothing deep, it's just a thing grandmas say to calm you down.
chat.meaning: In Markandeya's story, the world rests in God and is breathed out again. For Hindus, a pause is a rest before the next breath, not the end.

tie.story: Markandeya was breathed into the child on the banyan leaf, saw the whole world held inside, and was breathed out again.
tie.friend: Priya's freeze at the stop sign was a pause, not the end: she can breathe and drive on.
tie.you: what feels over in your life, but might be a rest?

kumbhaka.meaning: the pause in the breath, held gently at the top or bottom

kumbha.meaning: a pot, a clay water jar

Markandeya.meaning: a sage who saw the whole world inside a child

Vishnu.meaning: the god who keeps the world, resting on the ocean between worlds

Bhagavata Purana.meaning: a collection of stories of Vishnu and Krishna

pralaya.meaning: the dissolving of the world at the end of an age

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 12.8–12.9 (Markandeya's vision of the child on the banyan leaf)
Hindu teaching of cyclical creation and dissolution (pralaya)

notes: Hatha Yoga Pradipika dated to about the 15th century (Svatmarama); 'about five hundred years ago' — some date it slightly later. Confirm.
Antara (inner) and bahya (outer) kumbhaka; kevala kumbhaka as effortless retention (HYP 2.71–2.74). Yoga Sutras 2.50 name bahya and abhyantara; 2.51 the fourth. Confirm terms.
Safety guidance (pregnancy, high blood pressure, heart or lung conditions; stop if anxious) is conservative general advice; confirm with a qualified teacher.
Outline says 'gentle holds'; two-count holds chosen.
